patient.name: Sofia Mendes
patient.setting: GP surgery, later the Emergency Department
patient.complaint: Weight loss, palpitations and feeling hot and shaky for 3 months
background: Non-smoker; hopes to start a family next year

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with weight loss, heat intolerance, tremor and tachycardia: the age, the goitre (diffuse, nodular, single, tender) and the eyes decide the cause. Thyroid storm and AF also appear.

points: Sofia, 29, has lost **6 kg** while eating more.
Feels **hot** when colleagues are cold; sweats through her shirts.
Heart races; hands shake when she signs documents.
Loose stools, light periods, snapping at her partner.

steps.lead: Sofia's body is **running fast**: excess thyroid hormone drives her metabolic rate up and makes her sympathetic system overactive.

points: Warm, moist palms and a **fine tremor** of outstretched hands.
Smooth, **diffuse goitre** with a soft bruit.
Brisk reflexes; lid lag on looking down.

steps.lead: Sofia ticks the symptom list and the signs: **tachycardia**, fine tremor, warm moist skin, goitre, hyperreflexia and lid lag.

visual.title: Sofia's rhythm strip
visual.caption: Sinus tachycardia at 118 bpm. In an older patient, thyrotoxicosis often shows as new AF.

steps.lead: A young woman with a **smooth, diffuse goitre** and type 1 diabetes points to **Graves'**. Nodules suggest Plummer's; a painful goitre suggests De Quervain's.

steps.q: Which sign, if present, would be most specific for Graves' disease?
steps.r: **Exophthalmos** (plus pretibial myxoedema and acropachy) comes from TSH receptor antibodies, so it is specific to Graves'. The others occur with any cause.

steps.lead: Sofia has overt disease. A **low TSH with normal T4** would be subclinical, and hoarseness with a neck mass would need urgent surgical referral.
If Sofia stopped treatment or caught an infection, she could tip into **thyroid storm**: fever, delirium, very fast heart rate and vomiting.

steps.text: Lid lag and lid retraction happen in **any** thyrotoxicosis (sympathetic drive). Only **proptosis**, pretibial myxoedema or acropachy prove Graves'.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' (TFTs), 'confirm the diagnosis' (TSH receptor antibodies), and the uptake scan pattern that names the cause.

steps.q: Which test should Sofia have first?
steps.r: **TFTs** are first-line and gold standard: prove thyrotoxicosis before looking for the cause.

steps.title: Sofia's bloods
steps.text: Suppressed TSH, high T4 and T3, TRAb positive: Graves'. A baseline FBC before carbimazole.

steps.lead: Sofia's **suppressed TSH with high free T4 and T3** confirms primary thyrotoxicosis.

visual.title: Free T4
visual.label: Sofia 42
visual.caption: High T4 with a suppressed TSH. A normal T4 with low TSH would be subclinical.

steps.lead: Sofia's **positive TSH receptor antibodies** confirm Graves', so she does not need an uptake scan.
If Sofia's TRAb were negative, an **uptake scan** would name the cause by its pattern.
Sofia's TSH is suppressed, as expected. A **raised TSH** with high T4 would point to the pituitary and need a **pituitary MRI**.

steps.text: Low uptake + painful neck after a cold = **De Quervain's**: the gland is leaking hormone, not making more, so antithyroid drugs do not help.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' (carbimazole plus propranolol), sore throat on carbimazole (stop, urgent FBC), pregnancy (PTU in the first trimester), definitive options, and thyroid storm.

steps.q: Which is the most appropriate initial treatment for Sofia?
steps.r: **Carbimazole** reduces hormone synthesis; **propranolol** controls the adrenergic symptoms while it takes effect.

steps.lead: Sofia starts **carbimazole** with **propranolol** for 12–18 months. She is warned: a **sore throat** means stop the tablet and get an urgent FBC.

visual.title: Sofia on carbimazole
visual.caption: Propranolol settles the heart rate quickly; carbimazole lowers T4 over weeks.

points: Week 6: sore throat and fever of 38.4°C.
She stops carbimazole and has a same-day FBC.

visual.title: Sofia's neutrophil count
visual.label: Sofia 3.8
visual.caption: Normal: a viral sore throat, so carbimazole restarts. Below 0.5 it would be agranulocytosis and stopped for good.

points: Month 4: she runs out of tablets during a chest infection.
Partner finds her **agitated and confused**, vomiting.

visual.title: ECG in the Emergency Department
visual.caption: Fast atrial fibrillation: irregularly irregular, no P waves.

steps.q: Sofia has thyroid storm. Which combination is most appropriate?
steps.r: Storm needs admission and **IV propranolol**, **PTU** (blocks synthesis), **steroids** (block T4 to T3) and supportive care.

steps.lead: Sofia is admitted for aggressive treatment, with fluids for her vomiting and fever. **Potassium iodide** can follow to block hormone release.
After the storm, Sofia chooses definitive treatment. **Radioiodine** is given once she has had **6–8 weeks** of antithyroid drug control.
**Thyroidectomy** is the alternative if Sofia relapses or has a large goitre. Its risks are **hypoparathyroidism** and **recurrent laryngeal nerve** damage.
Sofia wants a baby. In the **first trimester** she would need **PTU**, switching to carbimazole later. De Quervain's would need only NSAIDs.
Sofia's pathway follows **NICE** hyperthyroidism guidance: antithyroid drug plus beta-blocker, then definitive treatment by cause.

science.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely mechanism...?' for Graves' (stimulating antibody to the TSH receptor), nodules (autonomous somatic mutations), amiodarone (Jod-Basedow vs Wolff-Chaikoff), or tachycardia and AF (beta-receptor upregulation).

steps.lead: Sofia's tremor, sweating and racing heart come from a **higher metabolic rate** plus tissues that are **more sensitive to adrenaline**.

steps.title: Graves' in Sofia
nodes: IgG antibody binds the TSH receptor
Gland grows (diffuse goitre) and makes more T4/T3
Antibody ignores the feedback, so hormone stays high
steps.caption: The antibody acts like TSH, so the gland is driven no matter how low the real TSH falls.

steps.lead: Sofia's **TRAb** are IgG that mimic TSH, driving **diffuse hyperplasia** and hormone synthesis independent of feedback.
If Sofia had nodules, each one would be a clone with a **somatic mutation**, producing hormone whatever the TSH.

steps.q: Amiodarone causes thyrotoxicosis through which effect?
steps.r: **Jod-Basedow**: an iodine load drives uncontrolled synthesis. **Wolff-Chaikoff** is the iodine-induced shutdown that causes hypothyroidism.

steps.lead: Sofia is not on amiodarone, but it is the drug to look for: its **iodine** can push the gland either way.
Sofia's **AF at 164** came from excess T3 **upregulating beta-adrenergic receptors**, raising heart rate and output.
Running out of carbimazole plus a **chest infection** decompensated Sofia's thyrotoxicosis into storm.

mcq.q: What is the most common cause of thyrotoxicosis?
mcq.r: Graves' is most common overall, especially in young women; toxic multinodular goitre is second.

mcq.q: What is the most specific sign of Graves' disease?
mcq.r: Exophthalmos is specific to Graves'; lid lag can occur in any thyrotoxicosis.

mcq.q: Which cause gives a painful, tender goitre after a viral illness?
mcq.r: De Quervain's (subacute) thyroiditis is post-viral, painful and self-resolving.

mcq.q: What does the uptake scan show in toxic multinodular goitre?
mcq.r: Patchy uptake from several autonomous nodules.

mcq.q: A raised TSH with high free T4 suggests what?
mcq.r: Non-suppressed TSH with high T4 points to the pituitary: arrange pituitary MRI.

mcq.q: A patient on carbimazole develops a sore throat. What should happen?
o: Stop carbimazole and check FBC urgently
mcq.r: Sore throat may be agranulocytosis: stop the drug and do an urgent FBC.

mcq.q: Which antithyroid drug is first-line in the first trimester of pregnancy?
mcq.r: PTU in the first trimester (carbimazole is teratogenic early), then switch to carbimazole.

mcq.q: What are the two key risks of thyroidectomy?
o: Hypoparathyroidism and recurrent laryngeal nerve damage
mcq.r: Removing or damaging the parathyroids causes hypocalcaemia; RLN damage causes hoarseness.

mcq.q: What causes continuous overactivity in Graves' disease?
o: IgG antibodies stimulating the TSH receptor
mcq.r: Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins activate the TSH receptor independent of feedback.

mcq.q: Why does thyrotoxicosis cause tachycardia and AF?
mcq.r: Upregulated beta-receptors increase heart rate and cardiac output.

technique.stem: A 27 year old woman has a 4 month history of weight loss despite a good appetite, heat intolerance and palpitations. She has vitiligo. Her pulse rate is 112 bpm and BP 132/66 mmHg. She has a fine tremor, a smooth, diffuse, non-tender goitre with a bruit, and bilateral proptosis.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis: confirm thyrotoxicosis, then use the neck and eyes to find the cause.

clues: weight loss despite a good appetite
steps.x: Young woman, autoimmune background, diffuse goitre, and proptosis (the most specific sign).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Graves' disease.**

elim: De Quervain's has a painful, tender goitre and no proptosis.
Phaeochromocytoma gives episodic attacks and hypertension, no goitre.
A toxic adenoma is a single nodule.
TMNG is nodular, usually over 50, and has no proptosis.

steps.x: **B. Graves' disease.** Diffuse goitre + proptosis + young woman.

technique.stem: A 31 year old woman has a 2 month history of anxiety, weight loss and sweating. Her pulse rate is 106 bpm and BP 128/70 mmHg. She has a diffuse, non-tender goitre and no eye signs. Thyroid function tests show a suppressed TSH and raised free T4.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the cause?

steps.x: Thyrotoxicosis is proven; the question asks for the cause.

clues: suppressed TSH and raised free T4
steps.x: Primary thyrotoxicosis with a diffuse goitre: probably Graves'.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **TSH receptor antibodies** confirm Graves'.

elim: FNA is for a suspicious nodule.
Pituitary MRI is for a raised, not suppressed, TSH.
Thyroglobulin monitors differentiated thyroid cancer.
TPO antibodies are non-specific and also found in Hashimoto's.

steps.x: **E. TSH receptor antibodies.** TFTs prove it; TRAb names it.

technique.stem: A 34 year old woman with Graves' disease stopped her carbimazole 3 weeks ago. She now has a fever, vomiting and agitation. Her temperature is 40.1°C, pulse rate 172 bpm irregular, BP 164/70 mmHg and respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute. She is confused.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?

steps.x: Initial management of an acutely unwell thyroid patient.
Non-compliance, then fever, delirium and fast AF: **thyroid storm**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Admit: **IV propranolol + PTU + corticosteroids** with fluids.

elim: That is myxoedema coma treatment.
Storm is an emergency; she cannot go home.
Radioiodine is slow and is not emergency treatment.
Surgery in an uncontrolled storm is dangerous.

steps.x: **B. IV propranolol, PTU and corticosteroids.** Block action, synthesis and conversion.

technique.stem: A 45 year old man has a 2 month history of palpitations and tremor. He has been taking amiodarone for 18 months for ventricular tachycardia. His pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 134/80 mmHg. Thyroid function tests show a suppressed TSH and raised free T4.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his thyroid dysfunction?
o: Iodine load driving uncontrolled hormone synthesis

steps.x: Mechanism: the drug history is the key.

clues: suppressed TSH and raised free T4
steps.x: Thyrotoxicosis on an iodine-rich drug.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Jod-Basedow effect**: iodine excess drives uncontrolled synthesis.

elim: Anti-TPO destruction causes Hashimoto's hypothyroidism.
Iodine-induced shutdown is Wolff-Chaikoff, which causes hypothyroidism.
A TSH-secreting adenoma would not suppress TSH.
Viral release is De Quervain's, with a painful neck.

steps.x: **B. Iodine load driving uncontrolled synthesis.** Jod-Basedow = hyper; Wolff-Chaikoff = hypo.

practice.stem: A 68 year old woman has a 6 month history of weight loss, palpitations and anxiety. Her pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 142/78 mmHg. She has a fine tremor and an irregular goitre with several firm nodules. There are no eye signs. An isotope uptake scan shows patchy uptake.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: An older woman with a nodular goitre, TRAb negative and patchy uptake has toxic multinodular goitre (Plummer's). Graves' gives diffuse uptake.

steps.x: Cause of thyrotoxicosis: age, neck and scan.
Over 50, many nodules, patchy uptake.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Toxic multinodular goitre.**

elim: De Quervain's is painful with globally low uptake.
Graves' gives diffuse uptake and positive TRAb.
Hashitoxicosis is brief, with a non-tender diffuse goitre.
Toxic adenoma is a single hot nodule.

steps.x: **E. Toxic multinodular goitre.** Second most common cause; patchy uptake.

practice.stem: A 38 year old woman has a 10 day history of neck pain radiating to her jaw, palpitations and sweating. She had a sore throat and cough 3 weeks ago. Her temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 108 bpm and BP 124/74 mmHg. The thyroid is diffusely enlarged and very tender.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A painful, tender goitre after a viral illness with thyrotoxicosis and a high ESR is De Quervain's (subacute) thyroiditis; uptake would be globally reduced.

steps.x: Diagnosis: the painful neck is the discriminator.

clues: neck pain radiating to her jaw
sore throat and cough 3 weeks ago
steps.x: Post-viral, painful, tender thyroid with thyrotoxicosis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **De Quervain's thyroiditis.**

elim: Anaplastic cancer is a rapidly growing hard mass in the elderly, not thyrotoxic.
Graves' is painless.
Hashimoto's goitre is non-tender.
A toxic adenoma is a painless single nodule.

steps.x: **B. De Quervain's thyroiditis.** Painful + post-viral + low uptake; treat with NSAIDs.

practice.stem: A 52 year old man has noticed a lump on the right side of his neck. He has lost 4 kg and feels hot and shaky. His pulse rate is 100 bpm and BP 138/80 mmHg. There is a single 3 cm smooth nodule in the right thyroid lobe. An isotope scan shows a single hot nodule with suppressed uptake in the rest of the gland.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: One autonomously functioning nodule that suppresses the rest of the gland is a toxic (solitary) adenoma. TMNG would show several hot areas.

steps.x: Cause of thyrotoxicosis with a neck lump.

clues: a lump on the right side of his neck
single hot nodule with suppressed uptake in the rest of the gland
steps.x: One hot nodule, rest suppressed.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Toxic adenoma.**

elim: Cancers are usually cold nodules and euthyroid.
Graves' gives diffuse uptake.
Thyroglossal cysts are midline and move with tongue protrusion.
TMNG shows patchy uptake in several nodules.

steps.x: **D. Toxic adenoma.** Single hot nodule.

practice.stem: A 41 year old woman with Graves' disease is brought to the Emergency Department 2 days after an emergency appendicectomy. She is agitated and vomiting. Her temperature is 40.3°C, pulse rate 168 bpm, BP 170/74 mmHg and respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute. She is disorientated and has a coarse tremor.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Hyperpyrexia, extreme tachycardia, hypertension and delirium in a Graves' patient after surgery is thyroid storm. Septic shock is hypotensive.

steps.x: Diagnosis in a hot, fast, confused patient.
Known thyrotoxicosis plus a surgical precipitant, now hyperpyrexic and delirious.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Thyroid storm.**

elim: Malignant hyperthermia occurs during anaesthesia, with rigidity.
NMS needs an antipsychotic and causes rigidity.
Phaeochromocytoma does not explain a free T4 of 68.
Septic shock causes hypotension.

steps.x: **E. Thyroid storm.** Precipitants: infection, surgery, non-compliance.

practice.stem: A 72 year old man has 2 weeks of palpitations and breathlessness. He has lost 5 kg over 3 months and feels hot. His pulse rate is 136 bpm irregularly irregular and BP 146/84 mmHg. He has a fine tremor. ECG (see item resources).

visual.title: 12-lead ECG
visual.caption: Irregularly irregular narrow-complex rhythm with no P waves.

practice.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of his ECG finding?
practice.e: New AF with weight loss, heat intolerance, tremor, suppressed TSH and high T4 is thyrotoxic AF from beta-receptor upregulation. Always check TFTs in new AF.

steps.x: Name the ECG, then its cause.
AF plus hypermetabolic symptoms and thyrotoxic bloods.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: AF caused by **thyrotoxicosis**.

elim: No alcohol history, and alcohol does not suppress TSH.
IHD does not explain weight loss and heat intolerance.
Mitral stenosis gives a diastolic murmur.
PE gives sudden breathlessness and pleuritic pain.

steps.x: **E. Thyrotoxicosis.** New AF: always check TFTs.

practice.stem: A 63 year old man has 6 weeks of weight loss, tremor and sweating. He has atrial fibrillation and has taken amiodarone for 2 years. He has no neck pain and no eye signs. His pulse rate is 98 bpm irregular and BP 132/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his thyrotoxicosis?
practice.e: Amiodarone's iodine load can cause hyperthyroidism (Jod-Basedow effect); it needs drug withdrawal where possible. TRAb negative and no eye signs argue against Graves'.

steps.x: Cause question: check the drug list.

clues: no neck pain and no eye signs
steps.x: Thyrotoxic on amiodarone, TRAb negative.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis.**

elim: De Quervain's has a painful neck.
TRAb negative and no eye signs.
Secondary disease would have a raised TSH.
No nodule is described.

steps.x: **A. Amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis.** Iodine excess, Jod-Basedow.

practice.stem: A 30 year old woman has a 3 month history of palpitations, weight loss and heat intolerance. Her pulse rate is 110 bpm and BP 130/68 mmHg. She has a fine tremor and warm, moist skin.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
practice.e: TFTs are first-line and gold standard for suspected thyrotoxicosis. The uptake scan identifies the cause once TFTs are abnormal.

steps.x: Initial investigation.

clues: palpitations, weight loss and heat intolerance
fine tremor and warm, moist skin
steps.x: Classic thyrotoxicosis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Thyroid function tests.**

elim: A 24 hour ECG assesses rhythm, not the cause.
Uptake scans come after TFTs.
Ultrasound is for nodules.
Metanephrines test for phaeochromocytoma, less likely with heat intolerance and weight loss over months.

steps.x: **B. Thyroid function tests.** Prove it first.

practice.stem: A 46 year old woman has a 2 month history of palpitations and weight loss. Her pulse rate is 102 bpm and BP 128/74 mmHg. Her thyroid is mildly enlarged and non-tender, with no discrete nodules. There are no eye signs. TSH receptor antibodies are negative.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to establish the cause?
practice.e: With TRAb negative, the uptake scan distinguishes Graves' (diffuse), toxic multinodular goitre (patchy) and thyroiditis (globally reduced). Pituitary MRI is for a raised TSH.

steps.x: Cause still unknown after TFTs and antibodies.
Primary thyrotoxicosis, cause unclear.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Thyroid isotope uptake scan.**

elim: CT neck is for retrosternal goitre or malignancy staging.
FNA is for a suspicious nodule.
Her TSH is suppressed, so this is not pituitary.
She is symptomatic now; waiting does not find the cause.

steps.x: **E. Thyroid isotope uptake scan.** Diffuse, patchy or low uptake names the cause.

practice.stem: A 26 year old woman has newly diagnosed Graves' disease. She has weight loss, tremor and palpitations. Her pulse rate is 116 bpm and BP 128/66 mmHg. She has no eye signs and is not pregnant. Her full blood count is normal.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: First-line is carbimazole (12–18 months in Graves') with propranolol for adrenergic symptoms. Radioiodine comes after 6–8 weeks of antithyroid drug control.

steps.x: Initial management of new Graves'.
Symptomatic, not pregnant, no neutropenia: carbimazole is safe.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Carbimazole and propranolol.**

elim: Levothyroxine treats hypothyroidism.
PTU is for the first trimester or storm; iodide is for storm.
Radioiodine follows 6–8 weeks of drug control.
Thyroidectomy is a last resort.

steps.x: **A. Carbimazole and propranolol.** Block synthesis, control symptoms.

practice.stem: A 33 year old woman started carbimazole for Graves' disease 5 weeks ago. She now has a severe sore throat and mouth ulcers. Her temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 118/70 mmHg. Her pharynx is inflamed.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Continue carbimazole and give oral penicillin
Stop carbimazole and arrange an urgent full blood count
practice.e: A sore throat and fever on carbimazole may be agranulocytosis: stop the drug and check an urgent FBC. Switching to PTU is unsafe because it can also cause agranulocytosis.

steps.x: Next step for a new symptom on a known drug.

clues: started carbimazole for Graves' disease 5 weeks ago
severe sore throat and mouth ulcers
steps.x: Sore throat with fever early on carbimazole: think agranulocytosis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Stop carbimazole, urgent FBC.**

elim: Continuing risks fatal neutropenic sepsis.
Any dose can cause agranulocytosis.
Waiting a week is unsafe.
PTU can also cause agranulocytosis; check the FBC first.

steps.x: **D. Stop carbimazole, urgent FBC.** Sore throat on carbimazole = FBC today.

practice.stem: A 30 year old woman with Graves' disease is 7 weeks pregnant. She has palpitations and heat intolerance. Her pulse rate is 108 bpm and BP 116/68 mmHg. She is not taking any medication. She has no eye signs and a diffuse goitre.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate antithyroid treatment?
practice.e: PTU is first-line in the first trimester because carbimazole is teratogenic early; switch to carbimazole in the second and third trimesters. Radioiodine is contraindicated in pregnancy.

steps.x: Drug choice in pregnancy: check the trimester.
First trimester, thyrotoxic, untreated.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Propylthiouracil.**

elim: Carbimazole is contraindicated in the first trimester.
Lithium is teratogenic (Ebstein's anomaly).
Radioiodine is contraindicated in pregnancy.
Surgery is a last resort and avoided in the first trimester.

steps.x: **C. Propylthiouracil.** PTU first trimester, carbimazole after.

practice.stem: A 25 year old woman has weight loss, heat intolerance and a smooth diffuse goitre. Her pulse rate is 112 bpm and BP 130/64 mmHg. TSH is suppressed, free T4 is raised and an isotope scan shows diffuse increased uptake.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her hyperthyroidism?
o: IgG antibodies activating the TSH receptor
Release of stored hormone from damaged follicles
practice.e: Graves' is caused by thyroid-stimulating IgG that activates the TSH receptor, driving diffuse hyperplasia and synthesis independent of feedback. Release from damaged follicles gives low uptake.

steps.x: Mechanism: name the cause first.
Graves' disease.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IgG antibodies activating the TSH receptor.**

elim: Somatic mutations cause nodules with patchy or single hot uptake.
Pituitary excess would not suppress TSH.
No amiodarone or iodine exposure.
Thyroiditis gives globally reduced uptake.

steps.x: **C. IgG antibodies activating the TSH receptor.** Diffuse uptake = whole gland driven.

prompts.q: List the symptoms and signs of thyrotoxicosis.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: everything speeds up. Include the examination signs.

points.p: Weight loss with increased appetite, heat intolerance
Palpitations, tachycardia, AF
points.why: New AF in the elderly: check TFTs.

points.p: Fine tremor, anxiety, irritability
Sweating, warm moist skin, diarrhoea
Goitre, hyperreflexia, lid lag, menstrual irregularity
points.why: Lid lag is not specific to Graves'.

prompts.q: What are the causes of thyrotoxicosis and the clue for each?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: age, the shape of the goitre, pain and the drug list.

points.p: Graves': most common, young women, diffuse goitre, eye signs, TRAb
points.why: Exophthalmos is the most specific sign.

points.p: Toxic multinodular goitre (Plummer's): over 50, many nodules, patchy uptake
Toxic adenoma: single hot nodule
De Quervain's: post-viral, painful tender goitre, low uptake
Amiodarone (Jod-Basedow) and hashitoxicosis
points.why: Amiodarone can cause hypo- or hyperthyroidism.

prompts.q: Which features are specific to Graves' disease?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: what does TRAb do outside the thyroid?

points.p: Exophthalmos (most specific); eye involvement in up to 60%
Pretibial myxoedema
points.why: Plaques on the front of the shins.

points.p: Thyroid acropachy
Diffuse goitre with positive TSH receptor antibodies

prompts.q: What is thyroid storm, what triggers it, and what are the complications of thyrotoxicosis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: hot, fast, confused, with a trigger.

points.p: Storm: fever, tachycardia, delirium or agitation, vomiting and diarrhoea
points.why: Risk of heart failure and arrhythmia.

points.p: Triggers: infection, surgery, non-compliance
Subclinical (low TSH, normal T4): AF, osteoporosis, ?dementia
Hoarseness with a neck mass: urgent surgical referral
points.why: Possible malignant recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement.

prompts.q: How is thyrotoxicosis confirmed, and how is the cause found?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: prove it, then name it.

points.p: TFTs: low TSH, high free T4 ± T3 (first-line and gold standard)
TSH receptor antibodies support Graves'
Uptake scan: diffuse Graves', patchy TMNG, low De Quervain's
Raised TSH with high T4: secondary, pituitary MRI
points.why: TSH should be suppressed in primary disease.

prompts.q: What is first-line treatment, and what is the key warning?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: two drugs, one warning, one duration.

points.p: Carbimazole first-line
points.why: Contraindicated in the first trimester and neutropenia.

points.p: Propranolol for adrenergic symptoms
points.why: Works fast while carbimazole takes weeks.

points.p: Agranulocytosis: sore throat means stop and urgent FBC
Graves': 12–18 months of treatment
points.why: While awaiting definitive treatment or remission.

prompts.q: What are the definitive treatments, and how is pregnancy and De Quervain's managed?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: radioiodine then surgery; PTU in the first trimester.

points.p: Radioactive iodine after 6–8 weeks of antithyroid drug control
points.why: Definitive first-line for TMNG and toxic adenoma.

points.p: Thyroidectomy: risks hypoparathyroidism and RLN damage
points.why: For relapse, large compressive goitre or severe eye disease.

points.p: Pregnancy: PTU in the first trimester, carbimazole later
De Quervain's: NSAIDs, steroids if severe; postpartum: propranolol
points.why: No antithyroid drugs: the gland is leaking, not overproducing.

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: block the effect, the synthesis, the conversion and the release.

points.p: Admit; IV propranolol
points.why: Controls heart rate and adrenergic effects.

points.p: Propylthiouracil (or carbimazole)
Corticosteroids to block T4 to T3 conversion
Fluids, antiarrhythmics, potassium iodide
points.why: Iodide inhibits hormone release; lithium second-line.

prompts.q: Why does Graves' cause continuous overactivity, and why do nodules escape feedback?

points.p: IgG thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins activate the TSH receptor
Diffuse hyperplasia and synthesis independent of pituitary feedback
points.why: TSH is suppressed but the gland keeps going.

points.p: Nodules: somatic mutations cause TSH-independent production

prompts.q: Why does amiodarone cause thyroid dysfunction, and why does thyrotoxicosis affect the heart?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: two eponyms for iodine; one receptor for the heart.

points.p: Wolff-Chaikoff: iodine shuts down synthesis, hypothyroidism
Jod-Basedow: iodine drives uncontrolled synthesis, hyperthyroidism
Excess T3/T4 upregulates beta-adrenergic receptors
points.why: Explains tachycardia, AF and high-output heart failure.

points.p: Storm: catecholamine-potentiated hormone excess, decompensation
points.why: Triggered by infection, surgery or non-compliance.

glossary.Thyrotoxicosis: Too much circulating thyroid hormone from any cause.
glossary.Hyperthyroidism: Thyrotoxicosis caused by the thyroid gland overproducing hormone.
glossary.Graves' disease: Autoimmune hyperthyroidism caused by antibodies that switch on the TSH receptor.
glossary.TRAb: TSH receptor antibodies; their presence supports Graves' disease.
glossary.TSH receptor antibodies: Autoantibodies that stimulate the TSH receptor; positive in Graves' disease.
glossary.Toxic multinodular goitre: Enlarged thyroid with several autonomous nodules making excess hormone; usually over 50.
glossary.Plummer's disease: Another name for toxic multinodular goitre.
glossary.Toxic adenoma: Single autonomous thyroid nodule making excess hormone.
glossary.De Quervain's thyroiditis: Painful post-viral thyroid inflammation that leaks hormone; self-resolving.
glossary.Subacute thyroiditis: Another name for De Quervain's thyroiditis.
glossary.Hashitoxicosis: Brief thyrotoxic phase early in Hashimoto's thyroiditis.
glossary.Postpartum thyroiditis: Thyroid inflammation after childbirth, often with a thyrotoxic then hypothyroid phase.
glossary.Thyroid storm: Life-threatening decompensated thyrotoxicosis with fever, tachycardia and delirium.
glossary.Exophthalmos: Forward bulging of the eyes; the most specific sign of Graves'.
glossary.Pretibial myxoedema: Raised, waxy plaques on the shins in Graves' disease.
glossary.Thyroid acropachy: Finger clubbing with soft-tissue swelling in Graves' disease.
glossary.Lid lag: Upper lid slow to follow the eye down; occurs in any thyrotoxicosis.
glossary.Bruit: Whooshing sound heard with a stethoscope from turbulent blood flow.
glossary.AF: Atrial fibrillation: an irregularly irregular heart rhythm with no organised atrial activity.
glossary.Subclinical hyperthyroidism: Low TSH with normal free T4.
glossary.Secondary hyperthyroidism: Thyrotoxicosis driven by the pituitary, so TSH is raised or not suppressed.
glossary.Scintigraphy: Isotope uptake scan showing which parts of the thyroid take up tracer.
glossary.Carbimazole: First-line antithyroid drug that blocks thyroid hormone synthesis.
glossary.Agranulocytosis: Dangerously low neutrophil count; a rare serious side effect of carbimazole.
glossary.Propylthiouracil: Antithyroid drug inhibiting thyroperoxidase; first-line in the first trimester and in storm.
glossary.Thyroperoxidase: Thyroid enzyme that makes T4 and T3; blocked by antithyroid drugs.
glossary.Propranolol: Non-selective beta-blocker that controls adrenergic symptoms of thyrotoxicosis.
glossary.Radioactive iodine: Radioiodine taken up by the thyroid to destroy overactive tissue.
glossary.Thyroidectomy: Surgical removal of the thyroid gland.
glossary.Hypoparathyroidism: Low parathyroid hormone, causing low calcium; a risk of thyroidectomy.
glossary.Recurrent laryngeal nerve: Nerve to the voice box running next to the thyroid; damage causes hoarseness.
glossary.Potassium iodide: Iodine given in thyroid storm to block release of thyroid hormone.
glossary.Ebstein's anomaly: Heart defect of the tricuspid valve linked to lithium in pregnancy.
glossary.Wolff-Chaikoff effect: Iodine excess temporarily shutting down thyroid hormone synthesis, causing hypothyroidism.
glossary.Jod-Basedow effect: Iodine excess triggering uncontrolled hormone synthesis, causing hyperthyroidism.
glossary.Amiodarone: Iodine-rich antiarrhythmic that can cause hypo- or hyperthyroidism.
glossary.Somatic mutation: Gene change arising in one body cell, not inherited, that can make a nodule autonomous.
glossary.Beta-adrenergic receptors: Receptors for adrenaline on heart and other cells; increased by thyroid hormone.
glossary.High-output cardiac failure: Heart failure where the heart cannot meet a very high demand for output.
glossary.Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins: IgG antibodies in Graves' that bind and activate the TSH receptor.
glossary.ESR: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate, a blood marker of inflammation.
